sources.name: Cedric Nakamura
sources.quote: From behind the counter, you see two different crowds. The folks walking past on Telegraph are mostly new — younger, on their phones, heading to the tech offices or the pop-ups. The ones who actually come in are the regulars, the ones who've been here since before the rent signs went up. We get a few curious walk-ins, sure, but the people who buy records are the same faces I've seen for years. The block's moving faster than the store is, if that makes sense.

sources.name: Brady Lopez
sources.quote: Things have picked up some, sure. The lunch rush gets longer, and the coffee machine doesn't stop. But I'm in the back, elbow-deep in suds. I see the plates coming in, not the balance sheets. The bigger places, they've got their own rhythm, their own crowds. I just keep up with the dishes. It's a good job, steady. It pays the bills, and that's what matters.

sources.name: Derek Obi
sources.quote: I work at Oakland Tech Collective, so I'm on the side that feels the block moving. The building's got new people coming in all the time, and there's a hum to it. But when I walk past Art Walk Cafe or Night Walk Records, I see the same folks, the same pace. They're not standing still, but it's a different rhythm. I think the tech places bring a certain energy, but the small spots—they're the ones that make the block feel like a neighborhood. You watch them, and you wonder if they feel the same push we do, or if they're just holding on.

approvedQuotes.text: From behind the counter, you see two different crowds. The folks walking past on Telegraph are mostly new — younger, on their phones, heading to the tech offices or the pop-ups. The ones who actually come in are the regulars, the ones who've been here since before the rent signs went up. We get a few curious walk-ins, sure, but the people who buy records are the same faces I've seen for years. The block's moving faster than the store is, if that makes sense.

Things have picked up some, sure. The lunch rush gets longer, and the coffee machine doesn't stop. But I'm in the back, elbow-deep in suds. I see the plates coming in, not the balance sheets. The bigger places, they've got their own rhythm, their own crowds. I just keep up with the dishes. It's a good job, steady. It pays the bills, and that's what matters.

I work at Oakland Tech Collective, so I'm on the side that feels the block moving. The building's got new people coming in all the time, and there's a hum to it. But when I walk past Art Walk Cafe or Night Walk Records, I see the same folks, the same pace. They're not standing still, but it's a different rhythm. I think the tech places bring a certain energy, but the small spots—they're the ones that make the block feel like a neighborhood. You watch them, and you wonder if they feel the same push we do, or if they're just holding on.
